title: What are the Flink deployment modes — Session mode (long-running cluster, multiple jobs share it), Per-Job mode (dedicated cluster per job, YARN only, deprecated), and Application mode (job's main() runs on the cluster, preferred for production on K8s/YARN) — and when do you choose each?
shortTitle: What are the Flink deployment modes
topicTitle: What are the Flink deployment modes

s1_definition.profdef: Flink offers three deployment modes that differ in how clusters and jobs map to each other and where the job's main method runs. Session mode runs one long-lived cluster that many jobs submit to and share. Per-Job mode spins up a dedicated cluster for each job but runs the job's main method on the client, and it is deprecated. Application mode runs a dedicated cluster per application and executes the job's main method on the cluster itself rather than on the client, which gives the best isolation and resource behavior and is the preferred mode for production on Kubernetes and YARN.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India needs meeting rooms for processing tasks. Session mode is one big shared conference hall that stays booked all day, where many teams walk in and run their meetings side by side; convenient and quick to start a meeting, but teams can disturb each other and one messy team can hog the hall. Per-Job mode is booking a fresh private room for every single meeting, but the person who books it, the client, has to stand at the door doing the setup work for the whole time. Application mode is also a fresh private room per project, but now the setup work happens inside the room by the team itself, so the booking clerk at reception is free the moment the room is handed over, which is cleaner and more reliable for important production meetings.
s1_definition.oneliner: Session mode shares one long-lived cluster across jobs, Per-Job mode gives each job its own cluster with main running on the client and is deprecated, and Application mode gives each application its own cluster with main running on the cluster, which is preferred for production.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flink offers three deployment modes that differ in how clusters and jobs map to each other and where the job's main method runs. Session mode runs one long-lived cluster that many jobs submit to and share. Per-Job mode spins up a dedicated cluster for each job but runs the job's main method on the client, and it is deprecated. Application mode runs a dedicated cluster per application and executes the job's main method on the cluster itself rather than on the client, which gives the best isolation and resource behavior and is the preferred mode for production on Kubernetes and YARN.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India needs meeting rooms for processing tasks. Session mode is one big shared conference hall that stays booked all day, where many teams walk in and run their meetings side by side; convenient and quick to start a meeting, but teams can disturb each other and one messy team can hog the hall. Per-Job mode is booking a fresh private room for every single meeting, but the person who books it, the client, has to stand at the door doing the setup work for the whole time. Application mode is also a fresh private room per project, but now the setup work happens inside the room by the team itself, so the booking clerk at reception is free the moment the room is handed over, which is cleaner and more reliable for important production meetings.

**One line to remember:** Session mode shares one long-lived cluster across jobs, Per-Job mode gives each job its own cluster with main running on the client and is deprecated, and Application mode gives each application its own cluster with main running on the cluster, which is preferred for production.

sections.s2_technical:
The deployment modes answer two questions: how many jobs share a cluster, and where the job's main method executes, which matters because main is what builds the JobGraph and can be expensive or can download dependencies.

Session mode starts a single Flink cluster that stays running independently of any job, and you submit multiple jobs to it over time; they all share the same JobManager and TaskManagers and the same pool of slots. The advantages are fast job startup, because the cluster is already up, and efficient resource sharing for many small or short jobs, which makes it ideal for interactive exploration, ad hoc queries, and development. The disadvantages are weak isolation and shared fate: all jobs compete for the same slots, one job can consume resources others need, and a TaskManager failure can affect multiple jobs at once, while a problematic job can destabilize the shared cluster. So session mode trades isolation for convenience and is best for non-critical, many-job, interactive use.

Per-Job mode creates a brand-new dedicated cluster for each submitted job and tears it down when the job finishes, giving each job isolated resources so jobs do not interfere. However, in Per-Job mode the job's main method runs on the client that submits the job, so the client does the work of building the JobGraph and must have the dependencies, and the client stays involved, which is a bottleneck when submitting many jobs and couples the submission environment to the job. Per-Job mode was historically YARN-only and is now deprecated in favor of Application mode, which achieves the same per-job isolation without the client-side drawbacks.

Application mode also gives each application its own dedicated cluster, but it runs the application's main method on the cluster, specifically on the JobManager, rather than on the client. This means the client just ships the application jar and returns immediately, the expensive JobGraph construction and any dependency loading happen on the cluster, and the application is fully isolated with its own JobManager and TaskManagers. Because main runs on the cluster, a single application can even contain multiple jobs executed in sequence, all within its dedicated cluster. Application mode is the recommended mode for production, especially on Kubernetes and YARN, because it combines strong isolation, no client-side bottleneck, and clean resource lifecycle: the cluster exists for exactly one application and is cleaned up afterward. A senior-level nuance is the Kubernetes integration, where native Kubernetes application mode lets Flink itself request pods for the JobManager and TaskManagers, and the application is deployed as a self-contained unit, which fits cloud-native operations and GitOps. Another nuance is dependency handling: running main on the client in Per-Job mode means the client needs the user jars and can suffer from version conflicts and heavy local work, whereas Application mode isolates that on the cluster. The practical rule is to use session mode for development and many short interactive jobs, use application mode for production streaming and batch applications because of isolation and the cluster-side main, and avoid Per-Job mode since it is deprecated and application mode supersedes it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the data team ran all their Flink work, from a developer's quick exploratory job to the critical production fraud-scoring job, on one shared session cluster. When a developer submitted a heavy experimental job, it consumed slots the production fraud job needed, and once an experimental job crashed a TaskManager, the production job was disrupted too. This is exactly the isolation problem that choosing the right deployment mode solves: session mode shares fate across jobs, which is fine for development but wrong for critical production.

This is exactly how the modes differ. Session mode's shared cluster is convenient for many interactive jobs but offers weak isolation, while application mode gives the production job its own dedicated cluster so nothing else can starve or destabilize it.

Problem 2 — The team's older production setup used Per-Job mode, where the job's main ran on the submitting client, so the client machine did heavy JobGraph construction and needed all the dependencies, and submitting several jobs bottlenecked on that one client. Moving to application mode runs main on the cluster, freeing the client and isolating dependency work. This is the where-main-runs distinction and why application mode is preferred.

Because running Flink clusters is heavy, this runnable demo models the three modes. A `SessionCluster` is long-lived and accepts many jobs that share its slots, showing contention. A `PerJobDeployer` creates a cluster per job but runs main on the client, showing the client doing the work. An `ApplicationDeployer` creates a cluster per application and runs main on the cluster, showing the client returning immediately and full isolation. The demo submits a dev job and a production job under each mode to contrast isolation, client involvement, and fate sharing.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# flink-conf.yaml
execution:
  target: kubernetes-application   # session | per-job (deprecated) | application
kubernetes:
  cluster-id: fraud-scoring-app
  container:
    image: registry/bank-flink-fraud:1.0.0
taskmanager.numberOfTaskSlots: 4
```

Java source files:
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/flink-deploy-modes-1.0.0.jar com.bank.deploy.DeployModesDemo

# Real Flink CLI:
#   Session:     flink run -t remote fraud.jar          # submit to a running session cluster
#   Per-Job:     flink run -t yarn-per-job fraud.jar     # DEPRECATED
#   Application: flink run-application -t kubernetes-application \
#                  -Dkubernetes.cluster-id=fraud-app fraud.jar   # preferred for prod
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two jobs, a non-critical developer exploration job needing three slots and a critical production fraud-scoring job needing three slots, deployed under each of the three modes.

Step 1: In session mode a single long-lived cluster of four shared slots is started. The developer job is submitted and takes three of the four slots, starting quickly because the cluster is already up.

Step 2: The production fraud job is then submitted to the same session cluster, but only one slot is free, so it cannot get its three slots and must wait. This is the contention problem of a shared cluster: a non-critical job starved the critical one.

Step 3: A TaskManager failure is simulated in the session cluster, and the log shows it affects all running jobs on that shared cluster, illustrating the shared-fate weakness that makes session mode unsuitable for critical production.

Step 4: In Per-Job mode the production job is deployed with its own dedicated cluster, which gives isolation, but the log highlights that the job's main runs on the client, so the client builds the JobGraph and needs all the dependencies, and submitting many jobs would bottleneck on that one client. The log also notes Per-Job mode is deprecated.

Step 5: In Application mode the production job is deployed as its own application with a dedicated cluster, and the client simply ships the jar and returns immediately because main runs on the cluster. The JobGraph is built cluster-side, dependencies are isolated, the application is fully isolated with its own JobManager and TaskManagers, and the cluster lifecycle matches exactly this application and is cleaned up afterward, which is why it is preferred for critical production.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SESSION mode (shared, dev/interactive):
    job A ─┐
    job B ─┼──→ ONE long-lived cluster (shared slots) ──→ contention + shared fate
    job C ─┘        TaskManager failure → affects ALL jobs ✗ for prod

  PER-JOB mode (deprecated):
    client (builds JobGraph, holds deps) ──→ dedicated cluster per job ──→ isolated
    but many jobs bottleneck on the client ✗ ; main on CLIENT

  APPLICATION mode (preferred prod):
    client ships jar → returns immediately
         │
         ▼
    dedicated cluster per application
      main() runs ON CLUSTER (JobGraph built here, deps isolated)
      full isolation; lifecycle = this application only
      ✓ K8s/YARN production

  Choose: SESSION = dev/many-short ; APPLICATION = production ; PER-JOB = avoid (deprecated).
```

```
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Workload type → deployment mode                                 │

  Production fraud job → Application mode on Kubernetes:
    isolated JobManager + TaskManagers, self-contained, GitOps-friendly.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Deployment Mode Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Strategy: SessionCluster / PerJobDeployer / ApplicationDeployer   │
  │     differ in cluster-per-job and where main() executes            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: each deployer encapsulates one mode's lifecycle                │
  │  O: add a new target (e.g., standalone-application) independently  │
  │  L: all accept a FlinkJob and deploy it, interchangeable           │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │  FlinkJob     │───────▶│ SessionCluster        │ shared, long-lived
  │ - requiredSlots│ into  │ + submit()            │
  │ - critical    │        │ + taskManagerFailure()│
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘
                 ┌──────────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐
                 │ PerJobDeployer        │   │ ApplicationDeployer   │
                 │ main on CLIENT (deprec)│  │ main on CLUSTER (pref)│
                 │ + deploy()            │   │ + deploy()            │
                 └──────────────────────┘   └──────────────────────┘

  Key differences:
    SESSION:      clusters=1, jobs=many, main=client, isolation=weak
    PER-JOB:      clusters=per job, main=CLIENT, isolation=strong, DEPRECATED
    APPLICATION:  clusters=per app, main=CLUSTER, isolation=strong, PREFERRED

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. SessionCluster.submit(dev) → 3/4 slots
  2. SessionCluster.submit(prod) → waits (contention)
  3. SessionCluster.taskManagerFailure() → affects all
  4. PerJobDeployer.deploy(prod) → isolated, main on client (deprecated)
  5. ApplicationDeployer.deploy(prod) → isolated, main on cluster (preferred)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink has three deployment modes that differ in how jobs map to clusters and where the job's main method runs, which matters because main builds the JobGraph and may load dependencies. Session mode runs one long-lived cluster that many jobs submit to and share, so they all use the same JobManager, TaskManagers, and slot pool. Its advantages are fast job startup, since the cluster is already up, and efficient sharing for many small or short jobs, which makes it ideal for development, ad hoc queries, and interactive exploration. Its weakness is isolation and shared fate: jobs compete for the same slots, one job can starve others, and a TaskManager failure can hit multiple jobs at once, so it is wrong for critical production.

Per-Job mode creates a dedicated cluster for each job and tears it down afterward, giving isolation, but the job's main runs on the client that submits it, so the client builds the JobGraph and must carry the dependencies, which bottlenecks when submitting many jobs and couples the submission environment to the job. Per-Job mode was historically YARN-only and is now deprecated. Application mode also gives each application its own dedicated cluster, but it runs main on the cluster, specifically on the JobManager, so the client just ships the jar and returns immediately, the expensive JobGraph construction and dependency loading happen cluster-side, and the application is fully isolated with its own JobManager and TaskManagers, with the cluster lifecycle matching exactly one application. Application mode is the preferred mode for production, especially on Kubernetes and YARN, because it combines strong isolation, no client-side bottleneck, and a clean resource lifecycle, and native Kubernetes application mode lets Flink request its own pods as a self-contained, GitOps-friendly unit. So the rule is session mode for development and many short interactive jobs, application mode for production, and avoid Per-Job mode since application mode supersedes it.

At the National Bank of India we learned this painfully because we ran everything, from a developer's quick experiment to the critical fraud-scoring job, on one shared session cluster. A heavy experimental job once took the slots the fraud job needed, and when an experiment crashed a TaskManager it disrupted the production job too, which is the shared-fate weakness of session mode. Our older production setup had used Per-Job mode, where main ran on the submitting client, so the client did heavy JobGraph work and needed all the dependencies and became a bottleneck. We moved the critical fraud job to application mode on Kubernetes, which gave it its own dedicated, isolated cluster, ran main on the cluster so the client returned immediately and dependencies were isolated, and tied the cluster lifecycle to exactly that application. We kept a session cluster for developers' interactive work. That split, session for development and application mode for production, is exactly how I would advise choosing among the modes.
